rationale: A wins because it finds the non-obvious fourth story: "One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor" is the trade piece a real reporter could build around actual before/after data. B is competent, but it stays in the three obvious lanes and then oversteps with "Sweetgreen's own rollout is a concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" when the update only gives worries about reduced hours. A knows where the bodies are buried and labels the missing proof instead of decorating the hole.
gaps_in_A: "the beat that has watched automation live mostly in pilots and demo units" needs backing; that market-history claim is not in the supplied update.
"category-creation" is a little swollen. Sweetgreen making automation a default new-store format is a rollout story, not category creation unless you can prove the category shift.
"robot assembly its default store format" slightly rounds up "most new stores and retrofit some existing ones." Tighten it to default for most new builds.
gaps_in_B: "Sweetgreen's own rollout is a concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" is the bad overclaim. The update says some worry about reduced staff hours; it does not say reductions have happened.
It misses the strongest trade-depth route: a named retrofitted store with before/after throughput, labor hours, and margin data.
"Decay: 24hr" undersells the first two angles. Restaurant trades and finance desks can still use a week-long operations/profitability follow-up if the proof is fresh.

"a worker or labor advocate willing to speak; any union or labor-organization response" is plausible proof to seek, but it drifts toward a broader labor package before the core staffing facts are established.
